questions.q: A traction power failure is first detected at control through:
options: A passenger's phone call to the depot
The station master's weekly report
A Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) alarm, after which the Power Controller identifies the dead section and the trains standing in it
A drop in ticket sales
questions.explain: Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) sees the power system — identifying the dead section and its trains is step one.

questions.q: When power fails, trains in the dead section should first try to:
options: Coast to a station if possible; otherwise stand secured
Accelerate to build momentum through the section
Detrain passengers immediately wherever they stop
Reverse to the previous power section without instruction
questions.explain: A train at a station is always better than a train stranded in a section — coasting there is the first aim.

questions.q: While a train stands without traction power, its batteries keep which services running for a limited time?
options: Traction motors at full power
Lights and ventilation
The air-conditioning at full load
All station escalators
questions.explain: Battery backup covers lights and ventilation — it buys decision time, it does not move the train.

questions.q: The Power Controller's main restoration attempt is to:
options: Wait for the fault to clear itself
Order all trains to detrain passengers
Switch off the healthy sections as well
Isolate the fault and reconfigure the supply to feed the section from the healthy side
questions.explain: Like a home changeover switch at railway scale — feed the dead section from a healthy source.

questions.q: During a power failure, station essential services run on:
options: Backup power supply
Traction power borrowed from trains
Passengers' cooperation alone
No power at all until the grid returns
questions.explain: Stations are designed to keep essential services alive on backup during a traction/grid failure.

questions.q: If a power failure becomes prolonged, the planned outcome for a train that cannot be moved is:
options: Leaving passengers on board indefinitely
Asking passengers to find their own way along the track
Controlled detrainment of its passengers, with bus bridging arranged as needed
Running diesel vehicles into the tunnel immediately
questions.explain: Prolonged failure converts to a controlled detrainment — planned, staffed and protected.

questions.q: Service on the sections that still have power should be:
options: Stopped across the whole network automatically
Run into the dead section to pick up passengers
Increased to double frequency
Regulated — trains short-turned at the boundary of the dead section
questions.explain: The live network keeps working around the dead section, turning back at its edge.

questions.q: Why must service be restored gradually after a power failure, recharging step by step?
options: To give staff time to announce each train
To avoid a second trip caused by everything drawing power at once
Because trains forget their routes
To save the cost of electricity
questions.explain: A sudden full load can trip the supply again — gradual restoration protects the recovery.

questions.q: Passengers in a train standing without power most need:
options: Regular information and calm reassurance while lights and ventilation run on battery
Complete silence from the crew
Instructions to open windows and doors
A promise of the exact restoration minute
questions.explain: Information prevents panic in a dark, standing train — honest updates, not false promises.

questions.q: Detrainment during a power failure is prepared only when:
options: Ten minutes have passed in every case
A single passenger demands it
The train cannot be moved, or conditions inside it become unsafe
The power controller is on leave
questions.explain: Detrainment is a decision with conditions — immobility or unsafe conditions, not the clock alone.

questions.q: In the home-inverter comparison used for power failure, the Power Controller's role matches:
options: The battery that stores the charge
The electrician who tries the changeover to another supply
The fan that keeps running
The house owner who leaves home
questions.explain: Mains fail, battery carries the load briefly, the electrician reconfigures — the railway works the same way, bigger.

questions.q: A total telecom failure occurs between Operations Control Centre (OCC) and a section. The governing safety principle is:
options: No communication, no movement beyond the prescribed limits
Trains continue on timetable timings
Drivers use hand signals from passengers
Trains run faster to reach a working radio area
questions.explain: Movement authority travels by communication — when it cannot travel, movements stop or stay within strict limits.

questions.q: When the main radio/telecom channel fails, staff should fall back to:
options: Shouting between stations
Personal social-media messaging only
Waiting silently for the channel to return
Alternate channels — backup radio, telephone, fixed line, or runner/pre-arranged signals as per rules
questions.explain: The fallback ladder exists in the rules — communication is restored by another route, not by hope.

questions.q: During a telecom failure, train movements that cannot be communicated with safely should be:
options: Increased to clear the section
Left to each driver's choice
Reduced or stopped
Handed over to station staff permanently
questions.explain: If Operations Control Centre (OCC) cannot speak to a train, that train's movements shrink to what the rules safely allow.

questions.q: Why is a 'runner' or pre-arranged signal an acceptable last-resort communication method?
options: It is a laid-down fallback in the rules, so the message and its authority are still controlled
It is faster than radio
It needs no training
Passengers can also use it
questions.explain: Even the oldest fallback is rule-based — authority stays documented and controlled.

questions.q: A driver loses radio contact with Operations Control Centre (OCC) while approaching a station in normal running. He should:
options: Continue the whole journey as if nothing happened
Follow the prescribed failure procedure — proceed only as the rules permit and re-establish contact
Detrain passengers at the next signal
Reverse to the previous station
questions.explain: Communication failure has its own rule-book procedure — improvisation is not part of it.

questions.q: Which failure pair is correctly matched with its first control action?
options: Telecom failure — isolate traction power
Power failure — issue movement authorities by flag
Telecom failure — fall back to alternate channels and restrict movements
Signalling failure — arrange an ambulance
questions.explain: Each failure has its own first move — for telecom it is alternate channels plus restriction.

questions.q: During a power failure, why is keeping passengers informed especially urgent?
options: Passengers must vote on the next step
The Public Address (PA) system uses traction power
Information restores the power faster
Battery-backed light and ventilation are time-limited, and uninformed passengers in a dark train panic sooner
questions.explain: The battery clock is ticking — calm, informed passengers make the eventual decision easier and safer.

questions.q: A section loses power while two trains stand in it. Restoration priority for moving trains is decided by:
options: Operations Control Centre (OCC) with the Power Controller, based on position, passenger load and the reconfiguration plan
Whichever driver asks first
The train with the loudest passengers
The train nearest the depot gate
questions.explain: Recovery is planned centrally — position and load, not noise, set the order.

questions.q: After power is restored to a section, the first trains through should run:
options: At maximum speed to test the supply
As directed after restoration, building up gradually to normal service
Only after a full day's observation
Without passengers for a week
questions.explain: Gradual build-up proves the supply while the service returns.

questions.q: A telecom failure coincides with a signalling failure in the same area. The combined effect is:
options: No worse than a single failure
Easier, as staff have less to do
A reason to run trains on sight at normal speed
More restrictive than either alone — movements are limited to what can be authorised and communicated safely
questions.explain: Failures stack — when both protection and communication degrade, restriction deepens.

questions.q: Station staff lose all communication with Operations Control Centre (OCC) during an incident at their station. They should:
options: Wait doing nothing until contact returns
Evacuate the whole city network
Act under the local incident command as per rules, use any alternate channel, and protect trains and passengers
Ask passengers to relay messages by phone to Operations Control Centre (OCC) as official authority
questions.explain: Local command exists for exactly this gap — protection continues while communication is restored by other means.

questions.q: The correct order for handling a traction power failure is:
options: Detect through Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA), identify the dead section, try reconfiguration, regulate live sections, detrain only if prolonged or unsafe, restore gradually
Detrain everyone, detect, restore instantly, identify later
Restore at full load, identify, detect, regulate
Regulate, detrain, detect, restore, identify
questions.explain: Detect and identify come before decisions; detrainment is conditional; restoration is gradual.

questions.q: Why does the Power Controller isolate the faulty part before reconfiguring supply?
options: To punish the faulty equipment
So the fault cannot trip the healthy supply that will feed the section
Because isolation is needed for the report only
To darken the section for inspection
questions.explain: Feeding a live fault from a healthy source just spreads the failure — isolate first.

questions.q: A train stands in a tunnel without power and ventilation on battery is weakening. This pushes the decision towards:
options: Waiting indefinitely as batteries recharge themselves
Opening train doors into the tunnel without protection
Expediting restoration or moving to controlled detrainment before conditions become unsafe
Turning off the lights to save the battery for later
questions.explain: Worsening conditions inside the train are one of the two triggers for detrainment.

questions.q: During a prolonged power failure, bus bridging means:
options: Arranging buses to carry passengers around the affected section between stations
Buses entering the tunnel to collect passengers
Passengers walking on the road bridge above
Replacing all trains permanently with buses
questions.explain: Bridging keeps the journey possible while the railway section is out of service.

questions.q: Which statement about telecom fallback is correct?
options: Any movement is allowed once a mobile phone is available
Fallback channels remove all restrictions automatically
A runner can authorise unlimited movements
Movements may continue only within the limits the fallback communication can safely support
questions.explain: The fallback defines the limit — weaker communication means smaller, slower movements.

questions.q: A power failure affects only the traction supply; station lighting and Public Address (PA) still work on backup. Passenger handling should:
options: Treat the station as fully failed
Use the working station systems fully — announcements, guidance and orderly holding or detrainment
Close the station immediately in all cases
Stop all announcements to save backup power
questions.explain: Partial failure means using what still works — station systems are a resource in the response.

questions.q: The most dangerous response to a telecom failure would be:
options: Holding trains at stations
Using the telephone fallback
Continuing normal-speed movements with no communication between Operations Control Centre (OCC) and trains
Reducing the service frequency
questions.explain: Trains that the Operations Control Centre (OCC) cannot speak to cannot be protected — running at normal speed with no communication is the trap answer.

questions.q: After both power and telecom are restored following a combined failure, normal service resumes:
options: In a phased pattern after systems are tested and certified, with passengers informed
Instantly, the moment the lights return
Only after a week of trials
Without informing passengers, to avoid questions
questions.explain: Restoration is phased and certified for every system — power and communication alike.

questions.q: After a traction supply trip, the Power Controller recharges the section and it trips again immediately, twice in a row. This pattern most likely means:
options: The substation needs a rest
A permanent fault is present on the section (for example a fallen wire or a foreign object) — stop recharging, isolate the section and get it inspected
Passengers are overloading the trains
The timetable is too tight
questions.explain: A supply that trips once may be a passing fault; one that trips again on recharging is telling you the fault is still there. Repeated feeding into a permanent fault damages equipment and endangers staff.

questions.q: A train loses power and stops inside a neutral section (the short dead length of Overhead Equipment (OHE) between two feeding areas). Even after supply is restored to both sides, this train still cannot move on its own because:
options: Its driver has left
The neutral section itself carries no power by design — the train must be pushed or pulled out of it into a live section
Its brakes have locked permanently
The section has been closed for the day
questions.explain: A neutral section separates two power feeds and is always dead; trains normally coast through it on momentum. A train stranded inside it needs rescue to reach live Overhead Equipment (OHE).

questions.q: The Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) system of the power network itself fails, so the Power Controller can no longer switch supplies remotely. Working continues by:
options: Stopping all trains till the computers return
Sending staff to the substations to operate the switches locally, step by step on the Power Controller's instructions given over recorded communication
Letting each station switch as it likes
Feeding all sections from one substation at once
questions.explain: Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) is the remote-control layer, not the supply itself. When it fails, hands replace motors: local operation, one step at a time, under central instruction and full logging.

questions.q: To keep a dead section moving, supply is extended into it from the neighbouring substation (extended feeding). The price of this arrangement is:
options: Nothing — it is as good as normal supply
The extended feed has load limits, so fewer trains, reduced speed or both are imposed on that section
Trains must run in the opposite direction
Passengers must pay a surcharge
questions.explain: One substation doing the work of two can only carry so much load. Extended feeding keeps a thinner, slower service alive — it is a degraded mode, not a full cure.

questions.q: Only one train's radio set has failed while the rest of the network communicates normally. The correct handling of that train is:
options: Treat it as a total network failure and stop the whole line
Let it proceed cautiously to the next station, communicate there by fixed telephone or hand signals, and get the set repaired or the train replaced as directed by the Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Let it run the whole day without any radio
Ask its passengers to relay messages
questions.explain: A single failed set is a train defect, not a system failure. The train is nursed to a place where communication exists, and the Operations Control Centre (OCC) decides repair, withdrawal or continued working.
